depth: The monocular depth map shows a top-down egocentric view where the camera wearer stands facing forward and looking straight down at a floor (~3–5 m below the camera), with no other people present in the scene. The wearer's left arm (brightest white, ~3–5 m from the camera) and right arm (~3–5 m) extend from the bottom edge into the scene above their seated or standing legs (~3–5 m), surrounded by floor-level objects far out of arm's reach: an open rectangular container of dark hardware/fasteners straight ahead (~3–5 m), yellow and white wire coils ~3–5 m to its right, a small grey box beneath the right hand (~3–5 m), stacked cardboard boxes to the lower right (~3–5 m), and red tools and buckets to the left (~3–5 m). Across frames 1 to 4, the left hand moves up away from the container (~3–5 m away, partially occluding its interior and the yellow coil beneath it) while the right hand rests far from the lower grey box, and in frame 5 both hands descend farther from the camera (~3–5 m) and move apart centrally while holding a handful of fasteners above the container. Compared to RGB alone, the depth map clearly separates the vertical height of the elevated arms, knees, and tall container rims from the flat floor background and highlights the downward movement of both hands away from the camera in frame 5. However, the depth map is unreliable between the wearer's legs (producing a pitch-black void artifact), across the upper-left wall/floor corner in frames 1 and 5 where brightness shifts inconsistently, and inside the dark container where individual fasteners are flattened into a single smooth surface.
segmentation: The instance segmentation map isolates regions of the camera wearer's extended limbs in the foreground (~3–5 m from the camera) against an unsegmented black background, with no other people present and the wearer facing downward toward the floor. Across frames 1 to 4, it segments the left arm on the left (~3–5 m away, moving away from the upper container) and the right arm and legs on the right (~3–5 m away, separated by ~3–5 m laterally) as separate 'person' instances, before both hands diverge from the center at ~3–5 m depth in frame 5. The map provides sharp silhouettes for the wearer's arms that stand out more clearly than in the cluttered RGB floor scene, and in frames 4 and 5 it delineates the boundary of the open fastener container (~3–5 m ahead) and a small round bucket to the left (~3–5 m away, ~3–5 m left of the container). However, the map is highly unreliable in class labeling and completeness: it splits the single camera wearer into multiple fragmented 'person' masks that bleed onto the floor and coiled wires in frames 1, 2, and 4, and completely misses the wire coils, tools, and cardboard boxes on the right. Furthermore, it misclassifies the fastener container as a 'book' in frame 4 and a 'cell phone' in frame 5, a small white bucket on the left as a 'cup' in frame 5, and a corner of a cardboard box at the bottom-right (~3–5 m away) as a 'remote' in frames 2 and 3.
pose: The pose map renders only two magenta 2D hand skeletons on a black background, as the camera wearer's torso and head are behind the egocentric viewpoint and no other people are in the scene. In frames 1 to 4, both hands remain far out of arm's reach (~3–5 m from the camera and ~3–5 m apart vertically in the image plane), with the left hand positioned higher and slightly left while moving away from the fastener container (~3–5 m deep) and the right hand positioned lower and to the right (~3–5 m deep) resting atop the grey box. Between frames 1 and 4, the left hand's finger keypoints curl inward from an open splay (frames 1–3) into a closed pinch (frame 4) as it grasps a cluster of fasteners, while the right hand remains stationary in a curled posture. In frame 5, both hands move away from each other and downward away from the camera (~3–5 m away), diverging from the middle of the frame with their fingers curling around the transferred fasteners from opposite sides. This skeletal representation makes exact finger articulation, thumb opposition, and the transition from open reaching to pinching much easier to read than in the dark interior of the container in the RGB strip, though it is completely unreliable for tracking the wearer's visible legs and forearms (which lack yellow body skeletons) and suffers from self-occlusion where the fingers overlap the fasteners in frames 4 and 5.
